title: Design & Innovation — Chapter 1: The Digital Economy
subtitle: EPITA D&I4DBT Class 1. Concept-focused questions on today's digital economy, technology adoption and the S-Curve, the adoption lifecycle, information industries and dominant designs, the fundamental laws (Shannon, Moore, Metcalfe, Reed) and their consequences, general-purpose technologies, digital transformation, and the productivity paradox. Emphasis on reasoning and situational understanding rather than attribution.

questions.question: Which set of attributes best characterizes today's digital economy as presented in the course?
options: Loosely connected and independent, with no dominant players
Highly interconnected and interdependent, with strong dependency on a few dominant players
Fully decentralized with equal market power across all firms
Isolated local markets with little cross-border data flow
questions.explanation: The course frames the digital economy as highly interconnected and interdependent, yet concentrated around a few dominant players. The other options understate either the interdependence or the concentration of power that characterizes it.

questions.question: Information and data are described with the 'new oil / new currency' metaphor. Why is that metaphor considered apt?
options: Because data, like oil, is a finite fossil resource that will run out
Because data has become a core value-bearing resource that is extracted, refined and exchanged to create economic value
Because data can only be traded on commodity exchanges
Because data physically powers electrical grids
questions.explanation: The metaphor captures data's role as a primary source of economic value — gathered, processed and exchanged like a strategic commodity. It is not about physical scarcity, commodity-exchange trading, or literal energy generation.

questions.question: How has the digital economy evolved structurally, according to the course?
options: From a hyperconnected global system back into isolated local machines
From self-contained local machines into a hyperconnected system of interrelated heterogeneous entities governed by different, possibly conflicting logics
From a single centralized mainframe into one unified global rulebook
From analog markets into a fully standardized digital monopoly
questions.explanation: The trajectory runs from isolated, self-contained machines toward a hyperconnected web of heterogeneous entities operating under different and sometimes conflicting logics. The other options reverse the direction or wrongly imply unification under a single logic.

questions.question: In the old-economy versus new-economy comparison, why is the new economy associated with 'increasing returns' while the old economy shows 'diminishing returns'?
options: Because the new economy is asset-heavy and the old economy is asset-light
Because in the asset-light, information-driven new economy each additional user or unit can add value at near-zero marginal cost, unlike asset-heavy production with rising marginal costs
Because diminishing returns only apply to software
Because increasing returns require physical scarcity of goods
questions.explanation: The new economy is asset-light and information-driven, so scaling adds value at very low marginal cost (increasing returns), whereas asset-heavy production faces diminishing returns. The first option inverts the asset characterization; the others misstate where increasing returns come from.

questions.question: The slides note the time to reach a one-billion valuation fell from about 20 years to about 5 years. What best explains this acceleration?
options: Stricter regulation slowing competitors
Increasing returns and network effects that let asset-light digital firms scale far faster than asset-heavy incumbents
Higher physical manufacturing capacity
A reduction in the number of internet users
questions.explanation: Asset-light digital firms benefit from increasing returns and network effects, compressing the time needed to reach massive valuations. Regulation, manufacturing capacity and shrinking user bases would slow growth, not accelerate it.

questions.question: What does the course mean by stating it is 'no longer about new versus old economies'?
options: The old economy has completely vanished
Digitalization is blurring traditional sector borders and absorbing the divide between non-digital and digital economies
The new economy has failed and the old one returned
Both economies have merged into a single regulated market
questions.explanation: The point is that digitalization dissolves the boundary between digital and non-digital, blurring sector borders rather than one economy replacing the other. Neither economy has simply vanished, failed or merged under one regulator.

questions.question: The course links today's digital economy to which broader characterization of industrial change?
options: The Second Agricultural Revolution
The Digital Revolution or Fourth Industrial Revolution
The Bronze Age transition
The Green Revolution
questions.explanation: Today's digital economy is framed as part of the Digital Revolution, also called the Fourth Industrial Revolution. The other revolutions refer to unrelated historical transformations.

questions.question: Which statement about the materiality of the digital economy matches the course's nuance?
options: It is completely immaterial and consumes no physical resources
It is highly virtual but not so immaterial, since it still depends on physical infrastructure and energy
It is purely physical with no virtual component
It is immaterial only in developing economies
questions.explanation: The nuance is that the digital economy is highly virtual yet not truly immaterial — it relies on datacenters, devices, networks and energy. Claiming it is wholly immaterial or wholly physical misses this point.

questions.question: The course lists which two categories of forces shaping the digital economy?
options: Government subsidies and consumer fashion trends
Technology adoption by businesses and individuals, and fundamental underlying laws and principles with their consequences
Advertising budgets and tax policy
Weather patterns and demographic decline
questions.explanation: The two forces are technology adoption (by businesses and individuals) and the fundamental laws and principles together with their consequences. The other pairs are not the structuring forces the course identifies.

questions.question: Among the consequences of the fundamental laws, which list matches the course?
options: Higher taxes, slower internet, fewer devices, shorter innovation cycles
Convergence of networks/interconnectedness, the rise and present-day divergence of the internet, affordability of technologies, and long innovation cycles
Decline of networks, rising hardware costs, and the end of innovation
Fragmentation of standards, more expensive technology, and stable industries
questions.explanation: The consequences include convergence and interconnectedness, the internet's rise and current divergence, affordability of technologies, and long innovation cycles. The distractors reverse these trends (e.g., rising costs, slower internet).

questions.question: What phenomenon does the technology S-Curve describe?
options: Constant linear growth at a fixed rate
Slow initial growth, then rapid acceleration, then eventual maturity and plateau
Immediate explosive growth followed by collapse
Permanent exponential growth with no limit
questions.explanation: The S-Curve captures slow uptake, a phase of rapid acceleration, and finally maturity/plateau. Linear, instantly explosive, or unbounded-exponential patterns do not match the characteristic S shape.

questions.question: Christensen's S-Curve analysis distinguishes between which two dimensions of technology?
options: Hardware versus software technologies
Component technologies versus architectural technologies
Cheap versus expensive technologies
Open-source versus proprietary technologies
questions.explanation: The distinction is between component technologies (improving the parts) and architectural technologies (recombining parts into new system designs). The other pairs are not the dimensions used in this S-Curve framing.

questions.question: A disk drive is used as an example of which S-Curve category, and why?
options: Architectural, because it reorganizes an entire system
Component, because it is a building block whose own performance improves along its S-Curve
Architectural, because it connects multiple networks
Neither, because storage is not a technology
questions.explanation: A disk drive is a component technology: a building block that follows its own performance S-Curve. It is not an architectural technology, which would be a new system-level configuration.

questions.question: An internet browser is cited as an example of which S-Curve category, and why?
options: Component, because it is a single isolated part
Architectural, because it recombines and orchestrates underlying components into a new system-level capability
Component, because it only improves hardware speed
Neither, because it is purely a consumer product
questions.explanation: A browser is an architectural technology: it integrates and orchestrates underlying components into a new way of accessing the web. It is more than an isolated component or a hardware-speed improvement.

questions.question: Why is the S-Curve said to be useful for understanding the digital economy?
options: It predicts exact revenue figures for any firm
It captures how technologies grow and mature, helping explain adoption dynamics across both component and architectural levels
It proves that all technologies grow forever
It measures only manufacturing cost
questions.explanation: The S-Curve explains growth-to-maturity dynamics and helps reason about adoption at component and architectural levels. It does not yield exact revenues, claim unlimited growth, or measure only cost.

questions.question: The chronological technology-adoption progression illustrated in the course moves through which sequence of computing eras?
options: Mainframe, analytical engine, smartphone, IBM PC compatible
Analytical engine/Turing machine, mainframe, IBM PC compatible, mobile smartphone
IBM PC compatible, mainframe, Turing machine, smartphone
Smartphone, mainframe, analytical engine, PC
questions.explanation: The progression runs from the analytical engine/Turing machine, to the mainframe, to the IBM PC compatible, to the mobile smartphone. The other orderings scramble this historical sequence.

questions.question: Why does distinguishing component from architectural technologies matter when forecasting disruption?
options: Because component improvements always cause industry collapse
Because an architectural innovation can disrupt an industry even when component technologies are already mature, by recombining them into a new system
Because architectural technologies never change
Because only component technologies follow an S-Curve
questions.explanation: Disruption often comes from architectural innovation — recombining mature components into a new design — not merely from component progress. Both levels follow S-Curves, and architectural shifts are precisely what can upend incumbents.

questions.question: In Rogers' Technology Adoption Lifecycle, why are 'innovators' the smallest adopter segment?
options: Because they adopt last, after the product is proven
Because they are the few risk-tolerant first movers who adopt before the technology is validated by the wider market
Because they never actually adopt the technology
Because regulation caps their number
questions.explanation: Innovators are the small group of risk-tolerant first movers who adopt before mainstream validation, which is why they form the smallest segment. They adopt first, not last, and are not limited by regulation.

questions.question: What is the correct order of segments in the Technology Adoption Lifecycle?
options: Early adopters, Innovators, Late majority, Early majority, Laggards
Innovators, Early adopters, Early majority, Late majority, Laggards
Laggards, Late majority, Early majority, Early adopters, Innovators
Innovators, Early majority, Early adopters, Laggards, Late majority
questions.explanation: The sequence is Innovators, Early adopters, Early majority, Late majority, Laggards. The other orderings misplace one or more segments.

questions.question: In Geoffrey Moore's Market Development Lifecycle, what does 'The Chasm' represent?
options: The decline phase when a product loses all customers
The gap between early-market visionaries/enthusiasts and the pragmatic mainstream market, where firms look for niches to cross over
The point of maximum revenue
The transition from laggards back to innovators
questions.explanation: The Chasm is the gap between early-market visionaries and the pragmatic mainstream, which firms bridge by targeting niches. It is not the decline phase, the revenue peak, or a reversal back to innovators.

questions.question: In Moore's refinement, which stage is characterized by 'new applications have been found and the market is experiencing growth'?
options: Main Street and End of Life
Bowling alley and Tornado
The Chasm and Early market
Decline and Maturity
questions.explanation: The 'bowling alley and tornado' stage marks the period when new applications take hold and the market grows rapidly. Main Street is later stabilization; the Chasm precedes growth; decline/maturity come afterward.

questions.question: In the course's own adoption framework, which sequence of phases appears along the revenue-growth-over-time curve?
options: Growth, Early stage, Decline, Maturity, Chasm
Early stage, the Chasm / uncertainty zone, Growth, Maturity, Decline
Maturity, Growth, Early stage, Decline, Chasm
Decline, Maturity, Growth, Chasm, Early stage
questions.explanation: The phases run early stage, the chasm/uncertainty zone, growth, maturity, and decline. The other orderings break this logical revenue-over-time progression.

questions.question: Class Assignment 1 asks students to position which kinds of items within the adoption cycle?
options: Word processors, spreadsheets, email, web browsers
Internet of Things, Artificial Intelligence systems, Big Data technologies, Blockchain
Television, radio, telephone, fax
LP records, cassettes, CDs, streaming
questions.explanation: The assignment places IoT, AI systems, Big Data technologies and Blockchain on the adoption cycle. The other lists are mature or legacy technologies not used in this exercise.

questions.question: Why is crossing 'the Chasm' typically difficult for a new technology?
options: Because innovators refuse to buy anything
Because early-market visionaries adopt for novelty, while pragmatic mainstream buyers demand proven references and whole-product reliability — a discontinuity in what each group values
Because the technology becomes cheaper after the chasm
Because laggards block all sales
questions.explanation: The chasm is hard to cross because visionary early adopters and pragmatic mainstream buyers have fundamentally different requirements; pragmatists want proven references and complete, reliable solutions. Pricing changes and laggard behavior are not the core obstacle.

questions.question: Why is it useful to segment adopters (innovators, early adopters, majorities, laggards) rather than treat the market as uniform?
options: Because every segment adopts at exactly the same time
Because different segments adopt for different reasons and at different times, which shapes how a technology diffuses and how it should be marketed
Because segmentation only matters for hardware
Because laggards determine the launch strategy
questions.explanation: Segmentation matters because each group has distinct motivations and timing, governing the diffusion pattern and the appropriate go-to-market approach at each stage. The market is not uniform, and the framing applies beyond hardware.

questions.question: In the telephone-technology discussion, which progression of switching/transmission technologies is illustrated?
options: Packet switching first, then circuit switching, then analog circuits
Analog circuits and circuit switching, then digital circuits and packet switching, then GSM, 4G, 5G
5G, then GSM, then analog circuits
Digital circuits first, then analog circuits, then no switching
questions.explanation: The progression moves from analog circuits with circuit switching to digital circuits with packet switching, and then to mobile generations GSM, 4G and 5G. The other options reverse the chronology.

questions.question: In the computer-technology discussion, which progression of man-machine interfaces is illustrated?
options: Tactile screen, then GUI, then mainframe, then PC
Binary logic and mainframe, then PC, then GUI, then tactile screen
GUI first, then binary logic, then tactile screen
PC, then tactile screen, then mainframe, then GUI
questions.explanation: Interfaces evolved from binary logic on the mainframe, to the PC, to the graphical user interface, to the tactile touchscreen. The alternatives scramble this order.

questions.question: Switchboard operators are cited as a job that disappeared from the telecommunications industry. What does this illustrate?
options: That telecom employment is unaffected by technology
That technological change (automated switching) can eliminate entire job categories within an industry
That manual switching is still the dominant method
That operators were replaced by accountants
questions.explanation: The disappearance of switchboard operators illustrates how automation can wipe out whole job categories as a technology matures. It is not evidence that employment is unaffected or that manual switching persists.

questions.question: Accounting clerks and typists are cited as jobs that disappeared from which industry, and why?
options: The telecom industry, due to fiber optics
The computer industry, because software and personal computers automated manual clerical and typing tasks
The energy industry, due to deregulation
The automotive industry, due to robotics
questions.explanation: These clerical roles disappeared in the computer industry as PCs and software automated record-keeping and document production. The other industries and causes do not match the example.

questions.question: Silicon Graphics, Digital Equipment Corporation and Sun are cited as computer-industry firms that did not survive. What general lesson does this convey?
options: That market leaders are permanently safe
That even prominent technology firms can fail when they do not adapt to shifts in dominant designs and platforms
That hardware firms never fail
That these firms never existed commercially
questions.explanation: Their decline shows that established, prominent firms can still fail when technological shifts and new dominant designs leave them behind. It contradicts any notion that incumbents are permanently safe.

questions.question: How is a 'dominant design' (Utterback) characterized in the course?
options: The cheapest design available on the market
The design that wins the allegiance of the marketplace and that competitors and innovators must adhere to in order to gain a significant following
The first prototype ever produced
A design mandated by government regulation
questions.explanation: A dominant design is the one that captures the market's allegiance, forcing competitors to conform to compete. It is defined by market acceptance, not by being cheapest, first, or legally mandated.

questions.question: Why are dominant designs described as useful for analyzing technology markets?
options: They guarantee that the best technology always wins
They help understand technology adoption and can signal the shape of the adoption lifecycle quite early in the cycle
They make all competing products identical forever
They only matter after a market has declined
questions.explanation: Dominant designs are useful because they clarify adoption dynamics and can be identified early, indicating how the lifecycle may unfold. They do not guarantee the technically best option wins, nor are they only relevant in decline.

questions.question: The audio-format timeline (LP record 1950, audio cassette 1970, audio CD 1980, audio streaming 2000) is used to illustrate what?
options: That formats never change once introduced
The succession of dominant designs, where each format becomes the standard before being displaced by the next
That older formats are always superior
That streaming was the first audio format
questions.explanation: The timeline shows a succession of dominant designs, each becoming the prevailing standard until displaced. It does not imply formats are static, that older is better, or that streaming came first.

questions.question: A key implication of information theory highlighted in the course is that:
options: A signal can never be recovered once any noise is added
A signal can be reconstructed at the receiving end even when partially altered by noise
Noise increases the amount of information in a signal
Digital signals cannot be transmitted over long distances
questions.explanation: Information theory shows a signal can be reliably reconstructed despite partial corruption by noise — the basis of robust digital communication. Noise does not add information, and digital signals clearly travel long distances.

questions.question: Information theory established a relationship that turned signals into what?
options: Analog waveforms only
Bits of information
Mechanical vibrations
Continuous voltages with no quantization
questions.explanation: The theory expressed information in bits, making it measurable and digitally encodable. The other options describe analog or non-quantized representations, which is the opposite of the bit-based formulation.

questions.question: In information economics, information is best defined as:
options: Any raw data regardless of context
The meeting between data and a problem, representing the value side
The total number of bits stored in a system
A synonym for noise
questions.explanation: Information is defined as the meeting of data and a problem — the value emerges when data answers a question. Raw data without a problem, or a mere bit count, is not yet information in this value-oriented sense.

questions.question: The course cites the argument that beyond a certain amount of data:
options: The amount of usable information keeps rising indefinitely
The amount of information actually diminishes
Data automatically becomes knowledge
Storage costs fall to zero
questions.explanation: Beyond a threshold, additional data can reduce usable information because of overload — more is not always better. It does not rise indefinitely, turn automatically into knowledge, or eliminate storage costs.

questions.question: What does Moore's Law state?
options: The cost of electricity halves every decade
The number of transistors on a chip (computing capacity) roughly doubles at a regular interval
Network value grows with the square of users
Bandwidth doubles every six months regardless of hardware
questions.explanation: Moore's Law concerns the regular doubling of transistor density / computing capacity on a chip. The square-of-users statement is Metcalfe's Law, and the others are unrelated claims.

questions.question: How did the stated doubling period in Moore's Law change between its 1965 and 1975 formulations?
options: From doubling every 2 years to doubling every year
From doubling every year to doubling every 2 years
From doubling every month to doubling every year
It remained doubling every 18 months throughout
questions.explanation: The original yearly-doubling estimate was revised to roughly every two years. The other options reverse the change or cite intervals not used in this revision.

questions.question: Which is listed as an implication of Moore's Law?
options: Networks become less valuable as they grow
Miniaturisation and the disappearance of the analogue/digital frontier, leading to cyber-physical systems
Information always diminishes with more data
Innovation cycles become shorter than one year
questions.explanation: Continued miniaturisation blurs the analogue/digital boundary and enables cyber-physical systems — a direct implication of Moore's Law. The other statements relate to different laws or contradict the course.

questions.question: Via cheaper sensors and processors, Moore's Law is said to have blurred the frontier between which two worlds?
options: Public and private
Analogue and digital
Hardware and marketing
Local and global
questions.explanation: Affordable sensors and processors dissolve the analogue/digital frontier, embedding computation into physical objects. The other pairs are not the boundary the law is said to erase.

questions.question: What does Metcalfe's Law state?
options: The value of a network is proportional to the number of its users
The value of a network is proportional to the square of the number of its users
The cost of a network doubles every two years
The value of a network is independent of its size
questions.explanation: Metcalfe's Law holds that network value scales with the square of the number of users, reflecting the growth in possible connections. Linear or size-independent value, or a cost-doubling claim, are incorrect.

questions.question: What does Reed's Law emphasize beyond Metcalfe's Law?
options: The cost of building network hardware
The importance of subgroups in network formation
The doubling of transistors over time
The reconstruction of signals under noise
questions.explanation: Reed's Law stresses the value created by the formation of subgroups within a network, which grows even faster than pairwise connections. The other statements belong to other laws entirely.

questions.question: According to the course, the implications of Metcalfe's and Reed's Laws stress that a network is not only infrastructure but also:
options: A purely technical artifact with no economic role
A market / industry arrangement
A government monopoly
A temporary phenomenon
questions.explanation: These laws imply a network functions as a market or industry arrangement, not merely as physical infrastructure. It is neither purely technical nor inherently a monopoly or temporary.

questions.question: Network effects, per the course, help explain how which two things occur?
options: How hardware is manufactured and how chips are etched
How economic value is generated in information-driven industries and how technology adoption is influenced by social dynamics
How taxes are collected and how budgets are set
How signals are encoded and how noise is removed
questions.explanation: Network effects illuminate both value generation in information industries and how social dynamics drive adoption. The other pairs describe manufacturing, fiscal, or signal-processing topics, not network effects.

questions.question: Which set of laws and principles does the course group under 'fundamental laws and their consequences'?
options: Newton's laws, Ohm's law, and Kepler's laws
Information theory, Moore's Law, Metcalfe's Law, and Reed's Law
Supply and demand, comparative advantage, and elasticity
Boyle's law, Charles's law, and the ideal gas law
questions.explanation: The grouped laws are information theory, Moore's Law, Metcalfe's Law and Reed's Law. The other sets come from physics or general economics, not this framework.

questions.question: Why is 'affordability of technologies' presented as the first consequence of the fundamental laws?
options: Because regulation forces prices down
Because the exponential improvement in computing (Moore's Law) steadily drives down the cost of technology, making it widely accessible
Because demand for technology is falling
Because affordability is unrelated to the fundamental laws
questions.explanation: Affordability follows directly from Moore's-Law-driven exponential gains that reduce cost per unit of computing, broadening access. It is a consequence of the laws, not of regulation or falling demand.

questions.question: The second consequence of the fundamental laws concerns:
options: Fragmentation of all networks
Convergence of information networks
The end of the internet
A return to analog broadcasting
questions.explanation: The second consequence is the convergence of information networks, as voice, data, images and sound move onto common digital infrastructure. The distractors describe the opposite of convergence.

questions.question: The course characterizes 'the internet today' as the combination of which elements?
options: Only people and websites
People, companies, machines, software, data, and network traffic
Only cloud platforms and mobile apps
Only connected sensors and routers
questions.explanation: The internet today combines people, companies, machines, software, data and network traffic. The other options capture only a narrow slice of this composition.

questions.question: What does the course mean by saying today's internet is 'diverging'?
options: That the internet is shutting down
That after a phase of convergence, distinct domains such as social networks, content/indexing, cloud computing and emerging IoT are branching out
That all services are merging into one platform
That the internet is reverting to analog
questions.explanation: Divergence means specialized domains branch out after the earlier convergence onto the internet. It is not a shutdown, a merge into a single platform, or a return to analog.

questions.question: Which examples does the course associate with the 'cloud computing' branch of the diverging internet?
options: Facebook, TikTok, LinkedIn
AWS, Azure, Google Cloud
Google Search, Netflix, Spotify
GSM, 4G, 5G
questions.explanation: Cloud computing is exemplified by AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. The other lists belong to the social-network, content/indexing, or telecom branches respectively.

questions.question: The 'long innovation cycles' consequence is grounded in the idea of creative destruction. What does creative destruction describe?
options: The gradual preservation of all existing industries
The process by which new innovations continually displace and replace older technologies and industries
The permanent stability of market leaders
The avoidance of any disruption through regulation
questions.explanation: Creative destruction is the ongoing displacement of old technologies and industries by new innovations, underpinning long economic cycles. It is the opposite of preservation, stability, or disruption-avoidance.

questions.question: According to the long-innovation-cycles slide, roughly how long are these technology-driven economic cycles, and which sequence of drivers is shown?
options: About 5 to 10 years: smartphones, apps, social media, AI
About 50 to 60 years: mechanization, railways, electricity & chemicals, automation, computers & internet
About 100 years: only electricity
About 20 years: railways then the internet only
questions.explanation: The cycles span roughly 50–60 years, driven successively by mechanization, railways, electricity and chemicals, automation, and computers and the internet. The other options misstate the duration or the sequence of drivers.

questions.question: Why does the course present convergence and then divergence as two stages of the same internet story?
options: Because they are unrelated and contradictory trends
Because media first converged onto a common internet infrastructure, and as adoption matured, specialized domains differentiated and branched out from it
Because divergence happened before any convergence
Because both terms mean exactly the same thing
questions.explanation: Convergence brought voice, data, images and sound onto a shared internet; maturing adoption then drove divergence into specialized domains. The stages are sequential and complementary, not contradictory, simultaneous-identical, or reversed.

questions.question: How is a General Purpose Technology (GPT) characterized?
options: By being narrow, fixed in performance, and isolated from other sectors
By pervasiveness, inherent potential for technical improvement, and innovational complementarities
By being cheap, disposable, and short-lived
By being limited to a single industry
questions.explanation: A GPT is marked by pervasiveness, ongoing potential for technical improvement, and innovational complementarities that spur innovation elsewhere. The distractors describe narrow, static, or single-industry technologies — the opposite of a GPT.

questions.question: Which examples of General Purpose Technologies does the course give?
options: The disk drive, the browser, the smartphone
Electricity, the computer, the internet
The LP record, the cassette, the CD
The telephone switchboard, the typewriter, the fax
questions.explanation: Electricity, the computer and the internet are the course's canonical GPT examples because each is pervasive, improvable and complementary across the economy. The other lists are components or specific products, not GPTs.

questions.question: Using electricity as a GPT example, why do General Purpose Technologies deliver their benefits with a delay?
options: Because they are banned at first by regulators
Because they require complementary innovations across the entire value chain, such as reorganizing work and adapting infrastructure
Because they are too cheap to be adopted
Because they only work in laboratories
questions.explanation: GPTs pay off slowly because realizing their value requires complementary innovations — reorganizing factories, retraining workers, adapting infrastructure. The delay is not due to bans, low price, or lab-only feasibility.

questions.question: Which technology is identified as the most important general-purpose technology of our era?
options: Blockchain
Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning
Virtual reality
3D printing
questions.explanation: Artificial intelligence, and machine learning in particular, is presented as the most important GPT of the current era. The other technologies are significant but not given that overarching GPT status here.

questions.question: What is the significance of classifying AI as a General Purpose Technology rather than a niche tool?
options: It means AI will have no measurable economic impact
It implies AI is pervasive, improvable and complementary, so its full benefits depend on broad complementary innovation and may arrive with a delay
It means AI is confined to a single industry
It means AI requires no complementary changes to deliver value
questions.explanation: Treating AI as a GPT implies economy-wide pervasiveness, continued improvement, and dependence on complementary innovation, with benefits that may be delayed. The distractors deny its breadth or its need for complementary change.

questions.question: Why does labeling a technology a GPT change expectations about its economic payoff?
options: Because GPTs deliver instant, isolated gains in one sector
Because GPTs are expected to have broad, economy-wide impact that materializes only after complementary innovations are in place, implying a lag before full payoff
Because GPTs never improve after launch
Because GPTs reduce the need for any further innovation
questions.explanation: Calling something a GPT signals broad, cross-sector impact realized after complementary innovations diffuse, so payoff lags rather than being instant or isolated. GPTs keep improving and spur, rather than reduce, further innovation.

questions.question: What do 'innovational complementarities' mean in the context of a GPT?
options: That the GPT competes with and suppresses innovation elsewhere
That the GPT raises the returns to, and enables, innovation in many downstream sectors and applications
That the GPT can only be improved by its original creator
That the GPT requires no other technologies to function
questions.explanation: Innovational complementarities mean the GPT boosts and enables innovation across many downstream sectors, multiplying its impact. It does not suppress innovation, nor is it self-contained or improvable by only one actor.

questions.question: What does the course mean when it says 'all industries are going digital'?
options: That only the technology sector is affected
That digitalization is blurring traditional sector borders and absorbing the divide between non-digital and digital economies
That industries are becoming fully analog again
That all industries digitize at exactly the same pace
questions.explanation: Going digital means digitalization spreads across all sectors, blurring borders and dissolving the non-digital/digital divide. It is not limited to tech, nor uniform in pace, nor a reversal to analog.

questions.question: According to the Digital America (2015) framing, which sectors are best positioned to further digitize?
options: Agriculture and construction
Knowledge-intensive sectors such as ICT and media
Mining and heavy manufacturing
Hospitality and food service
questions.explanation: Knowledge-intensive sectors like ICT and media are best positioned to digitize further, given their information-centric activities. The other sectors face greater physical or capital constraints.

questions.question: The course stresses that in the race to digitalization, industries are:
options: All equally positioned and digitize at the same rate
Not all equal, with some better positioned than others
Unable to digitize at all
Required by law to digitize simultaneously
questions.explanation: Industries differ in their readiness and pace of digitization — some are better positioned than others. They are neither uniformly placed, incapable, nor legally forced to move in lockstep.

questions.question: After knowledge-intensive sectors, which sectors does the framing place next in digitization readiness?
options: Capital-intensive sectors first, then agriculture
Services sectors, then capital-intensive sectors
Only the public sector
Heavy manufacturing, then mining
questions.explanation: The ordering moves from knowledge-intensive to services sectors, and then to capital-intensive sectors. The other sequences misplace the tiers.

questions.question: Why are knowledge-intensive sectors (such as ICT and media) best positioned to digitize?
options: Because they rely on heavy physical assets that are easy to automate
Because their value rests on information and digital processes, which face fewer physical constraints and can be digitized more readily
Because they are the smallest sectors of the economy
Because they are exempt from competition
questions.explanation: Their information-based value and digitally native processes face fewer physical limits, making digitization easier and faster. It is not because they are asset-heavy, tiny, or shielded from competition.

questions.question: What is the 'productivity paradox' described in the information society?
options: Productivity grows faster than computing power
Productivity grows relatively slowly despite remarkable increases in computer power
Computing power falls while productivity rises
Productivity and computing power are perfectly correlated
questions.explanation: The paradox is that measured productivity grew slowly even as computing power surged. The other options misdescribe the relationship between productivity and computing power.

questions.question: What does the productivity paradox imply about the relationship between IT investment and measurable gains?
options: That IT investment instantly raises measured productivity
That large IT investment may not show up immediately in productivity statistics, partly because complementary organizational changes take time
That IT investment always reduces productivity
That productivity cannot be measured at all
questions.explanation: The paradox highlights a lag: heavy IT investment need not appear at once in productivity figures, in part because complementary organizational and process changes are required. It is neither an instant boost nor a guaranteed decline.

questions.question: What is the 'bottleneck' in the information society?
options: A shortage of data storage capacity
Human attention being overwhelmed by massive amounts of information, making attention a scarce resource
A lack of internet bandwidth
A shortage of computing hardware
questions.explanation: The bottleneck is human attention: an abundance of information overwhelms it, turning attention into the scarce resource. Storage, bandwidth and hardware are not the constraint emphasized here.

questions.question: The course links scarcity and value with which principle?
options: Abundance of everything makes everything valuable
Abundance of something creates scarcity elsewhere, and whatever is scarce becomes valuable
Scarcity has no effect on value
Value depends only on production cost
questions.explanation: The principle is that abundance in one resource shifts scarcity to another, and the scarce element gains value — which is why attention becomes valuable amid information abundance. The alternatives deny the scarcity–value link.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the 'several economies' the course says the digital economy comprises?
options: The Attention Economy
The Barter Economy
The Sharing Economy
The Platform Economy
questions.explanation: The several economies include attention, knowledge, sharing, subscription, platform and access economies — the barter economy is not among them. The other three options are explicitly part of the list.

questions.question: What is identified as the common element uniting the 'several economies' (attention, knowledge, sharing, subscription, platform, access)?
options: Government ownership
Adoption of digital technologies
Reliance on physical cash
Absence of any network effects
questions.explanation: What unifies these economies is that each is enabled by the adoption of digital technologies. They are not defined by state ownership, cash reliance, or the absence of network effects.

questions.question: In the concluding remarks, which are listed as OPPORTUNITIES of digital technologies?
options: Digital labor and loss of privacy
Engines of growth, and new industries and business models
Slower innovation and higher costs
Reduced connectivity and market fragmentation
questions.explanation: The opportunities highlighted are that digital technologies act as engines of growth and spawn new industries and business models. Digital labor and privacy loss are listed as challenges, not opportunities.

questions.question: Which are listed as CHALLENGES in the concluding remarks?
options: New business models and faster growth
Digital labor, privacy and protection of personal data, and whether public policy can keep pace with regulation
Cheaper hardware and broader access
Increasing returns and network effects
questions.explanation: The challenges include digital labor, privacy and personal-data protection, and the difficulty of public policy keeping pace through regulation. The other options describe opportunities or enabling mechanisms, not challenges.
